meta.title: Modernising a Global Issuer Processor: From Monolith to Amazon EKS | Panasa
meta.description: How Panasa moved a global issuer processor from EC2 monoliths to a container-based Amazon EKS platform with automated pipelines, IaC, and observability.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
The client is a global issuer processor supporting fintechs, banks, issuers, and corporates with card issuing, management, e-wallets, transaction processing, and multiple other services. They offer unified debit, credit, prepaid, and virtual card programmes in a single global architecture.

As digital transactions grew, the client needed to update its infrastructure and development workflows. It was running large, single-piece applications on Amazon EC2 virtual servers. That setup made deployments slow, limited how far the system could scale, and created extra work for the team. The client engaged Panasa to move its core applications to a container-based setup on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS), where each part of the application runs as a separate, independently deployable service.

sections.title: The Challenge
sections.body:
The client's existing setup could not keep up with the demands of a growing global payment platform. Five problems drove the need for change:

  • Deployments were slow, repetitive, and error-prone because teams had to set up EC2 servers by hand each time.
  • Adding capacity meant provisioning new EC2 instances manually, which cost more and took more time.
  • Sensitive credentials were stored in configuration files, and keeping the operating system patched introduced ongoing security risk.
  • Engineers had to configure load balancers manually for each server.
  • Logs and metrics were spread across many places, which made monitoring difficult and slowed down troubleshooting.

sections.title: Outgrowing your EC2 monolith?
sections.text: We migrate payment platforms to Amazon EKS with zero-drama cutovers. Here's how.

sections.title: Our Approach
sections.cardSummary: We moved the client's infrastructure to a container-based setup on Amazon EKS. Containers package an application and everything it needs to run, so teams can deploy consistently across environments. The work covered six areas.

steps.title: Containers & Automated Pipelines
steps.body: We moved the applications into Docker containers, stored the images in AWS ECR, and built automated pipelines in Bitbucket Pipelines to handle building, testing, and deploying without manual steps.

steps.title: Infrastructure as Code
steps.body: We used Terraform to define all AWS resources as code the team can review, version, and reuse, with Terraform Cloud workspaces keeping Dev, UAT, and Production consistent.

steps.title: Deployment Through Git
steps.body: We kept all Kubernetes deployment configuration in a dedicated Git repository, used Kustomize to adjust it per environment, and introduced ArgoCD to deploy changes automatically whenever the repository is updated.

steps.title: Observability
steps.body: We set up OpenTelemetry to collect logs, metrics, and traces, all flowing into Coralogix to give the team a single place to monitor the platform and investigate problems.

steps.title: Security & Governance
steps.body: We removed static credentials into AWS Secrets Manager, scoped permissions with IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA), and added SonarQube, Snyk, and Checkov to scan code, dependencies, and infrastructure before anything reaches production.

steps.title: Scaling & Traffic Management
steps.body: We set up Horizontal and Vertical Pod Autoscalers to add or reduce capacity as transaction volume changes, and used an Ingress Controller and API Gateway to manage incoming traffic securely, with QA testing automated in the pipeline.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: By moving from EC2 monoliths to a container-based Amazon EKS platform, the client gained faster and more reliable deployments, elastic scaling for growing transaction volumes, centralised security and governance, and unified observability — a foundation built for the demands of a global payment platform.
